Yeah, that's a good question, and honestly it's something I've reflected on quite a bit.

When we started OctoML, the motivation came very directly from the research side, from TVM. The core idea was that machine learning models need to run on a huge variety of hardware, from cloud GPUs to phones to little embedded devices, and the engineering effort to make each model run efficiently on each piece of hardware was just enormous. So with TVM we were trying to automate that: use machine learning compilation to take a model and generate optimized code for whatever target you have. The initial business thesis was pretty close to that. We thought, okay, companies will have models and they'll want to deploy them efficiently, so let's build a platform that makes that optimization and deployment easy.

What I learned over time is that the technology being valuable and the business being shaped exactly like the technology are two different things. In research you think in terms of the most general, elegant solution. In a company you have to think about who exactly is paying, what pain they feel right now, and how your product fits into how they already work. The landscape also shifted a lot while we were building. Generative AI and large language models came along, and suddenly the conversation wasn't about optimizing a vision model for an edge device. It was about serving these huge models cost-effectively at scale. So the company evolved more toward being an inference and serving platform, where the compilation and optimization are still underneath, but what customers interact with is closer to "give me a fast, affordable endpoint for this model."

For me personally, that was a really interesting lesson. The underlying belief, that ML systems and compilation matter a lot and that we should make models run everywhere efficiently, didn't change. But the way that belief turns into something people use and pay for has to adapt to the moment. It's also part of why I kept a foot in the open-source and academic world, with projects like MLC LLM. Some of those broader, more universal deployment ideas are maybe better served as open ecosystems, while a company has to focus on a narrower, very concrete problem. Both are important, they just play different roles.

fable-5.1.text:
When we started OctoML, the mental model was really a straight line from the research. We had built TVM at the University of Washington as a compiler stack, and the obvious thing was: take that compiler, make it a product, help people get their models running efficiently on whatever hardware they had. So the initial framing was very much "deployment optimization as a service." You bring a model, we compile it down, you get a faster, cheaper binary on your CPU or GPU or edge device.

What we learned pretty quickly is that the compiler is only one piece of what people actually struggle with. The hard part for most teams was not squeezing out the last twenty percent of latency; it was everything around that. Which hardware should I even be running on? How do I package this so it fits my serving stack? How do I keep it working as the model changes every week? The optimization was necessary, but it was not what people woke up worrying about.

And then the generative AI shift changed the landscape again. Suddenly the models were large language models and diffusion models, the workloads were dominated by a handful of architectures, and the question moved from "optimize my custom model" to "give me reliable, cost-effective inference for these big models at scale." That pushed the business toward something closer to an inference platform rather than a compiler tool. The technology underneath still mattered a lot, since efficiency is what makes the economics work, but the product surface became much more about the full serving experience.

So I would say the core thesis never really changed: machine learning deployment is a systems problem, and good systems make it cheaper and more accessible. What changed was where that value showed up. We started by thinking the value was in the compiler, and over time we understood the value was in abstracting the whole stack so users do not have to think about the compiler at all. In some sense, the better we did our job, the more invisible the original research became, and I think that is actually the right outcome.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is between the technology you want to build and the problem somebody needs you to solve. Initially, you tend to think about what the technology makes possible. But that doesn’t yet tell you what the business should be. You have to understand what people would actually use, what fits into their workflow, and what delivers enough value that they’re willing to pay for it.

So I wouldn’t necessarily think of the eventual business looking different as a departure from the original idea. The underlying motivation can stay consistent while the product changes quite a lot. The important thing is to stay open to learning what part of that idea matters to the customer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the way to think about it is that you start with a hypothesis about what the technology can enable, and then you have to learn what people actually need. Those two things don’t necessarily line up perfectly at the beginning.

Initially, you tend to think a lot about the technology: what can we make faster, what can we make easier? But building a business means understanding where that improvement matters enough for someone to adopt it and pay for it. That also includes all the things around the technology that make it useful to them.

So I wouldn’t necessarily view that difference as abandoning the original idea. The motivation can stay fairly consistent, while the product and the business model evolve as you learn.
